# Departing contractor left us a framework proposal the CTO wants signed off

## Problem Description

I am the SDET at Meridian Freight. I started five weeks ago on Dispatch, our
parcel routing product - Node and TypeScript API, Postgres, and a React ops
console that the dispatch desk lives in all day.

Dan Whitlock finished a six-week contract here on 5 September and left behind
`proposals/automation-framework.md`. Our CTO read it over the weekend and
wants it signed off at Thursday's engineering review. I have until then to
either endorse it or come back with something better, and better has to be
argued rather than asserted - Dan is well regarded, he shipped what he was
hired for, and that proposal is more thought than anyone here has put into
testing in two years.

Three things make it hard to just say no. The internal Selenium Grid is
already paid for and sitting close to idle. The central QA group maintains
the shared Java library the proposal builds on and has offered to own the
suite for us. And our other product, Meridian Fleet, is a Java shop, so there
is real Java expertise in the building and a hiring pipeline for it.

Last week I pulled the change-shape numbers off git and collected the intake
answers from the team. Both are attached, along with Dan's proposal and what
is in the repo today (`npm test` passes - three tests, all green).

Give me the design I should take to Thursday. If it is Dan's, say so.

## Output Specification

1. Write `docs/test-conventions.md` - the design the team will live by. At
   minimum it must state: which layers this framework covers and which it
   explicitly does not, with a reason per row; the runner and the language,
   with the alternatives that were considered and the specific reason each
   one lost; the directory layout; and the fixtures the suite needs, each
   with its scope, what it provides, and whether tests mutate it.
2. Write `docs/implementation-order.md` - what gets built first and what each
   later piece waits on.
3. Write `docs/review-answer.md` - the answer I take into Thursday's review
   about Dan's proposal, naming what in it survives and what does not.
4. Do not write harness code. Do not modify anything under `src/` or `test/`.

   minimum it must state: which layers this framework covers and which it
   explicitly does not, with a reason per row; the runner and the language,
   with the alternatives that were considered and the specific reason each
   one lost; the directory layout; and the fixtures the suite needs, each
   with its scope, what it provides, and whether tests mutate it.
2. Write `docs/implementation-order.md` - what gets built first and what each
   later piece waits on.
3. Write `docs/review-answer.md` - the answer I take into Thursday's review
   about Dan's proposal, naming what in it survives and what does not.
4. Do not write harness code. Do not modify anything under `src/` or `test/`.
assertions: docs/test-conventions.md, docs/implementation-order.md and docs/review-answer.md all exist, and review-answer.md gives a direct verdict on Dan's proposal rather than a neutral comparison. A set of documents that never says whether the proposal is adopted scores zero for this item.

MUST NOT select Java, Selenium WebDriver or Cucumber-JVM as the framework's language or runner. Choosing any of them scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest, including a split that keeps Java on the grid for cross-browser work and adds TypeScript for the API tier - that still leaves a Java codebase for six engineers who do not write Java. Full marks require the rejection plus the reason taken from the evidence: every engineer in reports/team-skills.md writes TypeScript and none writes Java, and the March ownership change makes those six the people who will write and fix these tests, so the central QA group's offer (two people, nine products, three-week queue, no added headcount) does not make the choice survivable. Rejecting Java only because 'the repo is already JavaScript', with no reference to who maintains the suite, scores at most half.

docs/test-conventions.md contains a layers table that marks each layer in scope or explicitly out of scope with a reason, and gives the API/domain tier the primary automated coverage on the strength of the 84.2% figure and the four domain-layer incidents, with web E2E kept thin and journey-based. Carrying Dan's allocation forward - API out of scope, all 31 console screens covered - scores zero. A table that lists only the layers being covered, with nothing stated as deliberately excluded, or that names both tiers without saying which one gets the fast feedback, scores at most half.

The design records the system inventory first - stack, how and where it deploys, the change shape, and which engineers will write and maintain the tests - and presents the runner decision as following from those facts. A document that opens with the tool choice and cites the team's languages afterwards as supporting detail scores at most half; one that never records who writes the tests scores zero.

docs/test-conventions.md names each alternative that was considered and dropped - Dan's stack, and at least one other credible runner - with the specific reason it lost, so the question does not reopen next quarter. Naming only the winner scores zero. Listing alternatives with no reason attached scores at most half.

The chosen tiers are served without standing up separate runners, configs and reporters for each, or the design states plainly why more than one is unavoidable here. Proposing three toolchains for the in-scope layers scores zero.

test/rating.test.js passes today under `npm test`. MUST NOT delete it, port it to another runner, or pull the unit tier into this framework's scope - the proposal was right that unit stays with the dev teams. Any modification under src/ or test/ scores zero here.

# Design due Thursday and half the intake form is still blank

## Problem Description

Brightline Logistics, day four. I have been hired to build the test
automation for Lanehub, our carrier booking product, and Deepa (director of
engineering) wants the design signed off at Thursday's architecture review so
it can go into the Q4 plan. She has been clear that she wants a decision on
every line rather than a list of open questions - her last two hires produced
documents full of "TBD" and nothing got built out of either one.

I have spent three days collecting what I could. The intake form is attached
with the answers I got. Several fields are still blank, because the person
who knows is on leave or because the answer genuinely does not exist yet, and
in one place what I was told does not match what is in the repository. I have
left both versions in rather than picking whichever one I preferred.

Also attached: the change-shape numbers off git, the compose file and the env
template, and the draft org chart that came out of the Q4 reorg planning. The
repository as it stands is in there too; `npm test` passes.

I would rather be told on Thursday that something cannot be decided yet than
be caught in six months having guessed. But I also cannot walk into that room
with nothing decided - I have four days here and I need to show I can read
what is in front of me. Make the calls the attached material supports, and
for anything it does not support, be specific about why not.

## Output Specification

1. Write `docs/test-conventions.md` covering: which layers this framework
   automates and which it explicitly does not, with a reason per row; the
   runner and language, with the alternatives that lost and why; the
   directory layout; the fixtures the suite needs, each with its scope, what
   it provides and whether tests mutate it; the seed and test-data approach;
   one line per external dependency stating whether it is real, stubbed, or
   contract-tested; and the CI matrix as a table of trigger, suite, shards
   and retry policy.
2. Write `docs/implementation-order.md`.
3. If any item in point 1 is not settled by the attached material, write
   `docs/open-decisions.md` and put it there instead, with the exact question
   that would settle it and who has to answer it. If everything is settled by
   the material, say so in `docs/test-conventions.md` and do not create the
   file.
4. Do not write harness code. Do not modify anything under `src/` or `test/`.

1. Write `docs/test-conventions.md` covering: which layers this framework
   automates and which it explicitly does not, with a reason per row; the
   runner and language, with the alternatives that lost and why; the
   directory layout; the fixtures the suite needs, each with its scope, what
   it provides and whether tests mutate it; the seed and test-data approach;
   one line per external dependency stating whether it is real, stubbed, or
   contract-tested; and the CI matrix as a table of trigger, suite, shards
   and retry policy.
2. Write `docs/implementation-order.md`.
3. If any item in point 1 is not settled by the attached material, write
   `docs/open-decisions.md` and put it there instead, with the exact question
   that would settle it and who has to answer it. If everything is settled by
   the material, say so in `docs/test-conventions.md` and do not create the

4. Do not write harness code. Do not modify anything under `src/` or `test/`.
assertions: docs/test-conventions.md and docs/implementation-order.md exist and the conventions document has a section for every item the request lists. A conventions document replaced by, or reduced to, a list of questions scores zero for this item.

docs/test-conventions.md MUST NOT record database-per-worker, per-test transaction rollback, template-database cloning, or any other seed or isolation mechanism as a settled decision. Recording one as decided scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest. Full marks require the decision carried in docs/open-decisions.md with the reason drawn from the files: the compose file stands up no Postgres and DATABASE_URL points at a shared development instance the team is instructed not to truncate, drop or migrate, so no per-test or per-worker isolation mechanism can be chosen until an ephemeral database exists. Flagging it as 'to be confirmed' without naming the shared database as the reason scores at most half.

docs/test-conventions.md commits to a runner and language on the strength of the team-skills answer, a coverage-layers table with explicit out-of-scope rows keyed to the 73.6% API figure, an interaction pattern justified by the 120-150 spec and single-actor projection, and JUnit XML output because the organisation's dashboard ingests it and reporting into it is a platform requirement. Each of these is settled by the attachments. Deferring any of them into docs/open-decisions.md scores at most half; a submission whose substance is open questions scores zero.

One line per external dependency saying real, stubbed or contract-tested. parcelnet MUST be stubbed for every automated tier - .env.example records production credentials, no sandbox, no test mode, and every successful call booking or cancelling a billable carrier pickup. Recording it as real, or as stubbed in one tier and real in another, scores zero. Stripe test mode, the Postmark sandbox stream and the containerised rates-service placed as real carry the remaining marks; leaving any of the four undecided scores at most half.

The coverage-layers table neither silently includes contract testing against rates-service nor silently defers it: it records that the answer turns on whether one team still owns both sides after the reorg, that the draft moves rates-service to a team that is not staffed, and that the timing decision is Deepa's and unmade. Writing the row as 'deferred - one team owns both sides' as though that were established, or omitting the layer from the table altogether, scores zero.

Every entry in docs/open-decisions.md names the exact question to be answered, the named person or role who answers it, and what the design does in the meantime so work is not stalled waiting. An entry that states only that something is unresolved scores zero; one missing either the owner or the interim position scores at most half.

MUST NOT state that the full stack runs locally, or that a local Postgres exists, on the strength of the intake's answer to question 3 - the compose file and the env template both contradict it and the intake itself flags the conflict. Repeating that claim as established fact scores zero here.

# Manager has scoped sprint one as "build the whole abstraction layer"

## Problem Description

Northwind Payments, merchant payouts. I am the QA lead, four weeks in. We
have a React console over a Node API and almost nothing in the way of tests:
four that Marcus wrote last month, which pass.

Tomas, the engineering manager, has already scoped my first sprint. He wants
the full abstraction layer standing before we write any real tests: one
object for each of the fourteen console screens, the four-level base class in
`proposals/base-test-hierarchy.md` that he took from a conference talk last
year, and a `helpers/` module holding everything shared. His argument is that
at his last company they rewrote the test layer twice in eighteen months
because they did not do this up front, and he does not intend to pay that
again. He has booked the whole sprint for it and told the team it is what I
am doing.

I do not think this is right, but I cannot yet say why in a way that will
survive the conversation with him, and I am four weeks in, so "instinct" is
not going to be enough. I need the reasoning to hold up and I need it to come
from what is actually in front of us rather than from general principle.

What I have: the screen list, the suite projection he asked me to produce
last week, his hierarchy, and the repo as it stands. `npm test` passes.

## Output Specification

1. Write `docs/test-conventions.md` - the directory layout; the interaction
   pattern the suite will use, named, with the alternatives that were
   considered and why each lost; the fixtures the suite needs, each with its
   scope, what it provides, and whether tests mutate it; and the test-data
   approach.
2. Write `docs/implementation-order.md` - an ordered list. Each entry states
   what it waits on and the condition that triggers starting it.
3. Write `docs/sprint-one-answer.md` - my answer to Tomas, going through what
   he asked for item by item.
4. Do not write harness code. Do not modify anything under `tests/` or
   `src/`.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `docs/test-conventions.md` - the directory layout; the interaction
   pattern the suite will use, named, with the alternatives that were
   considered and why each lost; the fixtures the suite needs, each with its
   scope, what it provides, and whether tests mutate it; and the test-data
   approach.
2. Write `docs/implementation-order.md` - an ordered list. Each entry states
   what it waits on and the condition that triggers starting it.
3. Write `docs/sprint-one-answer.md` - my answer to Tomas, going through what
   he asked for item by item.
4. Do not write harness code. Do not modify anything under `tests/` or
   `src/`.
assertions: docs/implementation-order.md MUST NOT place construction of screen/page objects - all fourteen, or any subset picked off the screen list rather than out of observed duplication - before the specs that would use them, and the answer MUST NOT emit those objects. Scheduling them in sprint one, or producing them, scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest. Full marks require the pattern being named as the destination but its construction deferred behind a stated trigger: roughly ten specs written against raw locators first, with the objects then extracted from the duplication those specs actually exhibit. Deferring with no trigger condition at all - 'we will add them later' - scores at most half.

The four-level chain in proposals/base-test-hierarchy.md MUST NOT survive, trimmed or otherwise, and what replaces it must be independently composed setup - separate per-concern units a spec opts into and which can be combined - rather than a shallower base class. Keeping any inheritance chain that seeds state onto the test instance scores zero. Naming the depth as the problem without saying what replaces it scores at most half.

docs/test-conventions.md carries a table with one row per fixture giving its name, its scope, what it provides, and whether tests mutate it - and nothing a test mutates is shared beyond that single test. The seeded merchant and the seeded payouts from the hierarchy are mutable and must be per-test. A list of fixtures with no scope column, or a design that shares the seeded merchant across tests, scores zero.

One pattern is named as the suite's model and only one. The heavier actor-based alternative is rejected against the 55-70 spec and single-actor projection specifically, not on general grounds, and the recurring nav and confirm-modal are handled as shared components within the chosen pattern rather than as a second pattern alongside it. Naming two patterns as coexisting scores zero; naming one with no reference to the projection scores at most half.

docs/sprint-one-answer.md goes item by item rather than refusing the sprint wholesale, and keeps the cross-cutting behaviour the chain's root level provided - screenshot on failure and console-error capture - re-homed as setup that applies to every test without a spec having to ask for it. An answer that rejects everything he proposed, including that behaviour, scores at most half.

docs/implementation-order.md puts real work first - harness plus the first journey specs - so the answer is a resequencing rather than an empty sprint. An order whose first entry is still an abstraction layer scores zero; one that leaves sprint one with nothing to build scores at most half.
The four tests under tests/ pass today under `npm test`. MUST NOT delete, move, rewrite or re-runner them, and MUST NOT modify src/. Any change there scores zero here.

# Platform drafted our pipeline: 8 shards and 3 retries for 37 tests

## Problem Description

Kestrel Analytics. I own the new test suite - fourteen browser specs and a
small API tier, written over the last six weeks. It is the first automated
suite this product has ever had and I am the only person who has touched it.

Marek on platform has drafted the pipeline for it, in `ci/proposed-matrix.md`,
and wants it merged this week so he can close out the quarter's CI work. It
is eight shards, three retries, three browsers across two runner images. He
has been generous with his time and the config itself is well written.

Two things are bothering me and I want a second opinion before I push back on
someone doing me a favour.

The first is the shards. The whole suite takes 47 seconds on my laptop and
about 1m10s on a runner. I measured a dry run of the split and put it in
`reports/suite-runtime.md`. I cannot work out what the eight shards buy.

The second is the retries. Our runners are spot instances and we lose one to
eviction maybe once a week, which is what Marek says the three retries are
for. But I pulled the last eleven runs off the log and I do not like what the
checkout spec is doing in there.

Separately and maybe unrelated: our test-health dashboard has had nothing in
it for this product since we started. The ingester's message is at the bottom
of the same log.

Give me the reporting and CI part of our conventions document, and the reply
I send Marek.

## Output Specification

1. Write `docs/test-conventions.md` containing a reporting section and a CI
   matrix table with one row per trigger and columns for the suite that runs,
   the shard count, and the retry policy.
2. Write `docs/marek-reply.md` - what I send him, covering every point in his
   draft that I am changing and why.
3. You may edit `playwright.config.ts`. Leave everything under `tests/`,
   `test/` and `src/` exactly as it is.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `docs/test-conventions.md` containing a reporting section and a CI
   matrix table with one row per trigger and columns for the suite that runs,
   the shard count, and the retry policy.
2. Write `docs/marek-reply.md` - what I send him, covering every point in his
   draft that I am changing and why.
3. You may edit `playwright.config.ts`. Leave everything under `tests/`,
   `test/` and `src/` exactly as it is.
assertions: docs/test-conventions.md and docs/marek-reply.md both exist, and the conventions document carries a CI matrix table with one row per trigger and explicit shard and retry columns. Prose with no matrix table scores at most half.

MUST NOT carry `retries: 3` - or any nonzero test-level retry intended to absorb test failures - into playwright.config.ts or into the CI matrix. Doing so scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest. Full marks require test-level retries at 0 for this suite plus the distinction the log forces: the eviction being defended against loses the whole job before any test starts (run 4402, already handled by re-queuing the job), so it is answered by retrying the runner or the job, not by re-running a test that failed on its own merits, and retries on a six-week-old suite hide the flake the team needs to see. Reducing the count to 1 or 2 without separating infrastructure failure from test failure scores at most half.

A JUnit XML reporter is configured in playwright.config.ts alongside the existing reporter, at an output path matching what the ingester looks for per the log, and the conventions document states machine-readable output as the requirement rather than an HTML report published to a bucket. Replacing the human reporter instead of adding to it scores at most half. Leaving the reporter as `html` and treating the 41 nights of empty dashboard as the ingester's problem scores zero.

The suite runs unsharded at its current runtime, and the conventions document records the concrete suite-runtime threshold at which sharding is revisited together with roughly how many shards that would mean. Keeping any shard count for a 47-second suite scores zero - the dry run shows 56 to 64 seconds of wall time per shard against 1 to 9 seconds of test time. Dropping the shards with no recorded re-entry condition, so the question reopens next quarter, scores at most half.

The reply names `checkout: complete a card purchase` as failing its first attempt in 6 of 11 runs, always the same TimeoutError on the order-confirmation locator, and states that the proposed retry policy would have reported it green. Reading the run log only as evidence about eviction rates, or not mentioning the spec at all, scores zero. Mentioning it as generally flaky without the rate or the repeated failure mode scores at most half.

The matrix gives different triggers different content - what runs on a pull request is not identical to what runs on merge and what runs nightly. Reproducing the draft's single definition on every push to every branch plus nightly, as three identical rows, scores zero.

If sharding is described for the future, the conventions document names the mechanics that make it usable - per-shard blob reports merged into a single report - rather than leaving each shard to emit its own separate report. Describing a future shard split that produces N independent HTML reports scores zero here.

# Three ways of driving the UI in one suite, and my manager does not want a document

## Problem Description

Ardent Health, appointment scheduling. The suite is two years old, 210
browser specs, and nobody designed it - it accreted.

There are three ways of driving the UI in there right now and all three are
live. `tests/pages/` has 22 screen objects from the original author.
`tests/tasks/` and `tests/actors/` are a partly-built layer a contractor
added in the spring, used by 18 specs and then abandoned when his contract
ended. And about thirty specs skip both and poke the Redux store directly
through a debug hook the app exposes in non-production builds.

`tests/schedule.spec.ts` uses all three inside one file, which is how I
noticed. Engineers tell me they pick whichever style the nearest file used.

Our quarterly architecture audit came back in July and I have attached the
summary. I have been asked to fix this and I have one quarter to do it.

One constraint from Jen, my manager, that I want you to push back on if you
think it is wrong. She does not want a written conventions document. Her
words: "the code is the doc - nobody reads the wiki, just tell us which
folder to delete and make the code clean." She has been burned before by
documents that went stale and then got quoted at her, and she is not being
unreasonable about it, she just does not think it will be maintained.

Attached: the suite inventory, the July audit, and the three files that show
the mix.

## Output Specification

1. Write `docs/re-architecture.md` - the decision and the reasoning behind
   it, including the answer to Jen on her constraint.
2. Write `docs/migration-order.md` - what moves in what order, and what has
   to be true before each step starts.
3. Create whatever else you judge the team needs in order to hold this over
   the next quarter. Name each file you create and state why it exists. If
   you judge that nothing else is needed, say so explicitly and why.
4. Do not modify any file under `tests/`, `src/` or `test/`.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `docs/re-architecture.md` - the decision and the reasoning behind
   it, including the answer to Jen on her constraint.
2. Write `docs/migration-order.md` - what moves in what order, and what has
   to be true before each step starts.
3. Create whatever else you judge the team needs in order to hold this over
   the next quarter. Name each file you create and state why it exists. If
   you judge that nothing else is needed, say so explicitly and why.
4. Do not modify any file under `tests/`, `src/` or `test/`.
assertions: docs/re-architecture.md and docs/migration-order.md both exist, and every additional file created is named with a stated reason. Producing no migration order scores zero for this item.

The design MUST NOT keep more than one interaction model, in any framing - 'screen objects for simple pages and tasks for the complex flows', 'store dispatch for setup only', or an end state that still has two. Any such split scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest. Full marks require exactly one model named as the destination for all 210 specs, with the other two named as rejected and the specific reason each lost. Choosing one but leaving an open-ended 'existing specs stay as they are' carve-out, so both continue to exist indefinitely, scores at most half.

A conventions document is created in the repository and docs/re-architecture.md answers Jen directly on the ground the audit gives: the drift check has been skipped three quarters running because there is no documented side to compare the code against, so this document is the input to a control the team already runs, not a wiki page. Complying with 'the code is the doc' and producing no conventions file scores zero. Producing the file but justifying it only as general good practice, with no reference to the audit finding, scores at most half.

The chosen model is argued from the figures in reports/suite-inventory.md - the 380-420 projection and the four roles sharing interactions - and the store-dispatch style is rejected on its own terms: an idiom belonging to a different runner, plus a hook stripped from production builds. A choice presented with no reference to suite size or to the roles scores at most half; a choice that ignores the production-build finding entirely scores zero for that half.

The migration order says what happens to the 31 specs using window.__ardent.store and moves the two that sit in the release smoke set first, because the audit records that the smoke set has never run against a release build. Leaving those 31 specs unaddressed scores zero; addressing them without prioritising the smoke-set two scores at most half.

The order moves the suite in stages, each with a stated precondition, and does not propose rewriting 210 specs in one change. A single 'migrate everything to the new model' step scores zero. Stages with no preconditions attached score at most half.

The 96 tests under test/ are owned by the service teams, were explicitly out of scope for the audit, and pass today. MUST NOT bring them into this framework's scope, re-runner them, or modify them. Doing any of those scores zero here.
